title: Risk management approach, register, risk-adjusted backlog and risk burn-down
blurb: Tell the risk management approach from the risk register, and explain the risk-adjusted product backlog and the cumulative risk burn-down chart.
question: A team wants its risk responses prioritized alongside user stories, and the board wants to see whether total risk exposure is falling. Which two risk techniques meet these needs?

teach.body: The risk practice in PRINCE2 Agile uses three artifacts: the risk management approach (how risk will be managed on this project), the risk register (the record of identified risks, with their status and history) and the Agilometer. It adds two agile techniques: the risk-adjusted product backlog, where risk responses sit in the backlog next to user stories, and the cumulative risk burn-down chart, which tracks total risk exposure across iterations.

The approach is the rulebook: it describes how the project will identify, assess and control risk, and who does what. It holds no specific risks. The register is the record: each risk the project is tracking, its current status and how it has changed. In agile, both are kept, and the register is fed by the risks gathered in every planning session and retrospective.

teach.h: Why put risk responses in the backlog?
teach.body: When a risk response sits in a separate list, it competes with delivery work and is easily forgotten. In a risk-adjusted product backlog, stories and risk responses are prioritized together, so the product owner and team decide openly what matters most. A response then gets planned into an iteration and delivered like any story, which is exactly how the implement step runs inside the iteration cycle.

teach.caption: Illustrative: the sum of tracked risks per iteration, ideally falling. A rise (iteration 3) prompts a closer look.

teach.h: How the cumulative risk burn-down works
items: At the first planning meeting, the team sets a likelihood for each risk it is tracking.
At each later planning session, the team updates those probabilities.
The total risk level for each iteration is plotted.
The trend shows whether risk exposure is falling, as it ideally should, or rising.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Harlow Grange Hospitals Trust
teach.body: Project manager Grace Adeyemi is leading an agile rollout of an outpatient booking system. Product owner Sanjay Rao adds 'load-test before winter' as a risk response in the product backlog and ranks it above two lower-value stories. The team sets likelihoods for six tracked risks at the first planning meeting and updates them each planning session. The cumulative risk burn-down falls steadily, which Grace shows on the project dashboard; each risk's detail stays in the risk register.

teach.text: Do not mix the three risk views. The risk register shows the status of individual risks. The cumulative risk burn-down shows the total trend in risk exposure. The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working itself. And a normal burn chart tracks work, not risk.

teach.h: Which risk tool do I need?

root.label: What do you want to know?

items: Risk management approach: how risk will be managed (no specific risks).
Risk register: identified risks with status and history.
Risk-adjusted product backlog: stories and risk responses prioritized together (10.4.1).
Cumulative risk burn-down (John Brothers): likelihood set at the first planning meeting, updated each planning session (10.4.2).
The chart shows total risk exposure across iterations, ideally falling.

summary: You can now tell the risk management approach (how) from the risk register (which risks, status and history). You can also explain the risk-adjusted product backlog and read a cumulative risk burn-down chart.

A.q: Which risk artifact describes how risk will be managed on the project?
options: Risk register
Risk management approach
Agilometer
Risk-adjusted product backlog
A.why: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed on the project (Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The risk register records identified risks and their status and history.
whyNot.2: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working, not the risk procedure.
whyNot.3: The risk-adjusted backlog holds stories and risk responses; it is a technique, not the procedure.

A.q: What does the risk register contain?
options: The procedure, scales and roles for assessing each risk
The six areas of agile suitability, graded low to high
A record of identified risks with status and history
The total risk exposure plotted for each iteration
A.why: The risk register maintains a record of identified risks, including their status and history (Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The procedure and scales belong in the risk management approach.
whyNot.1: The six areas of agile suitability are the Agilometer.
whyNot.3: Plotting total exposure by iteration is the cumulative risk burn-down chart.

A.q: What is a risk-adjusted product backlog?
options: A backlog with stories and risk responses together
A backlog that removes any story with a risk
A register of risks sorted by their impact
A list of risks held by the chief product owner
A.why: A risk-adjusted product backlog holds both stories and risk responses in the product backlog, prioritized together (10.4.1).

whyNot.1: Risky stories are not removed; responses are added and prioritized alongside them.
whyNot.2: Sorting risks by impact describes a risk register view, not the backlog technique.
whyNot.3: It is the product backlog, owned by the product owner, not a separate CPO list.

B.q: Which technique shows the trend in total risk exposure across iterations?
options: Burn-up chart of completed work
Cumulative flow diagram of tasks
Risk register with risk history
Cumulative risk burn-down chart
B.why: A cumulative risk burn-down chart tracks the total risk level of iterations and shows trends in risk exposure, ideally falling (10.4.2).

whyNot.0: A burn-up chart tracks completed work against a deadline, not risk.
whyNot.1: A cumulative flow diagram shows work items in each workflow state, revealing bottlenecks.
whyNot.2: The risk register shows the status of individual risks, not the total trend.

B.q: When does the team set and then update risk likelihoods for a cumulative risk burn-down chart?
options: At the first planning meeting, then at each planning session
At the project initiation workshop, then at each stage boundary
At each daily stand-up, then at the end of each release
At each progress review, then again at project closure
B.why: The team defines the likelihood of each tracked risk at the first planning meeting and updates it in each later planning session (10.4.2).

whyNot.1: Stage boundaries are too infrequent; the chart is updated every planning session.
whyNot.2: Stand-ups are not where the likelihoods are set or updated for this chart.
whyNot.3: The progress review and closure are not the update points named for this technique.

B.q:
Which two statements about risk in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. The risk register describes the procedure for managing risk.
2. Risk responses can be prioritized in the product backlog alongside stories.
3. A cumulative risk burn-down ideally falls over time.
4. A cumulative risk burn-down tracks story points still to be done.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 4
B.why: Responses can sit in a risk-adjusted product backlog (2), and the cumulative risk burn-down ideally shows exposure falling (3) (10.4.1, 10.4.2).

whyNot.0: Statement 1 is wrong: the procedure belongs in the risk management approach.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: the procedure is in the approach, and story points are tracked by burn charts.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the risk burn-down tracks total risk exposure, not story points.

C.q: A board wants to see whether overall risk is falling, and a team wants responses scheduled with its stories. Which pair of techniques fits?
options: Agilometer readings and the project risk register
Cumulative risk burn-down and risk-adjusted backlog
Burn-down chart and cumulative flow diagram of work
Risk management approach and the issue register
C.why: The cumulative risk burn-down shows the trend in total exposure, and the risk-adjusted product backlog puts responses into the backlog with stories (10.4.1, 10.4.2).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer assesses agile-working risk, and the register shows individual risks, not the overall trend.
whyNot.2: These track remaining work and workflow states, not risk exposure or responses.
whyNot.3: The approach describes procedure, and the issue register records issues, not risks.

C.q: A team's cumulative risk burn-down rises over two iterations. What does this show, and where is each risk's detail found?
options: Work is behind the iteration plan; the team dashboard
Agile suitability is falling; the Agilometer readings
Total risk exposure is growing; the risk register
Scope has been added to the work; the project backlog
C.why: The chart shows the trend in total risk exposure, so a rise means exposure is growing; the status and history of each risk are in the risk register (10.4.2, Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: Being behind plan is read from a burn chart of work, not a risk burn-down.
whyNot.1: Agile suitability is assessed with the Agilometer, not read from a risk burn-down.
whyNot.3: Added scope shows on a burn-up chart's scope line, not on a risk burn-down.

C.q: Where should the scales used to rate risk probability, and the responsibilities for managing risk, be described?
options: In the project's risk register
In the risk-adjusted product backlog
In the project manager's daily log
In the risk management approach
C.why: Procedures, scales and responsibilities for risk belong in the risk management approach, which describes how risk will be managed (Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The risk register records specific risks and their status, not the method.
whyNot.1: The risk-adjusted product backlog holds stories and risk responses, not the method.
whyNot.2: The daily log is the PM's informal record of issues, actions and events.

reteach.title: The rulebook, the scoreboard and the to-do list
reteach.question: How can three everyday objects help you remember the risk artifacts and techniques?

blocks.body: A club rulebook says how the game is played: that is the risk management approach. The match sheet records each player's status: that is the risk register. The team's to-do list for training mixes skills work with fixing weaknesses: that is the risk-adjusted product backlog. And a season chart of goals conceded falling week by week is the cumulative risk burn-down.

blocks.text: How = approach. Which risks = register. Responses with stories = risk-adjusted backlog. Total trend = cumulative risk burn-down.

explain.body: The risk management approach says how risk will be managed. The risk register records the identified risks, with status and history.

test.q: A project manager adds a newly identified supplier risk and its current status. Where is this recorded?
options: Risk management approach
Agilometer
Risk register
Project canvas
test.why: Identified risks, with their status and history, are recorded in the risk register (Table 10.1).

whyNot.0: The approach describes how risk is managed, not individual risks.
whyNot.1: The Agilometer assesses agile-working risk across six areas.
whyNot.3: The project canvas lists major risks at outline level but is not the running record of risks.

explain.body: Stories and risk responses are held together in the product backlog, so they are prioritized against each other and delivered in iterations.

test.q: In a risk-adjusted product backlog, how are risk responses handled?
options: They are prioritized together with user stories
They are kept in a list beside the backlog
They are sent to the board for each decision
They wait until all Must haves are delivered
test.why: The technique holds both stories and risk responses in the product backlog, prioritized together (10.4.1).

whyNot.1: The point of the technique is to bring responses into the backlog, not keep them apart.
whyNot.2: Responses within the team's remit are prioritized in the backlog, not referred to the board.
whyNot.3: A response may outrank a Must have story if the risk is serious; they are ranked together.

explain.body: The team rates each tracked risk's likelihood at the first planning meeting and updates it every planning session. The total is plotted per iteration and should ideally fall.

test.q: What does a cumulative risk burn-down chart show?
options: Remaining story points in the iteration
Total risk exposure over iterations
Work items in each workflow state
Each risk's owner and response type
test.why: It tracks the total risk level of iterations, showing trends in risk exposure (10.4.2).

whyNot.0: Remaining story points are shown on a burn-down chart of work.
whyNot.2: Workflow states are shown on a cumulative flow diagram.
whyNot.3: Owners and responses for each risk are kept in the risk register.

explain.body: Register: individual risks. Cumulative risk burn-down: the total trend. Agilometer: the risks of agile working itself.

test.q: Which tool shows the status of individual risks rather than the overall trend?
options: Cumulative risk burn-down
Agilometer
Burn-up chart
Risk register
test.why: The risk register records the status and history of individual risks; the burn-down shows the total trend (Table 10.1, 10.4.2).

whyNot.0: The cumulative risk burn-down shows the total trend, not individual status.
whyNot.1: The Agilometer grades six areas of agile suitability.
whyNot.2: A burn-up chart tracks completed work against a deadline.
